question: According to the Kentucky CDL manual, what is the most important reason for inspecting your vehicle?
choice_a: Safety, for yourself and for other road users
choice_b: To avoid a parking ticket
choice_c: To keep the vehicle's paint looking new
choice_d: To satisfy the vehicle's warranty
explanation: The manual states that safety, for yourself and other road users, is the most important reason to inspect your vehicle.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Why Inspect

question: What is the minimum tread depth required in every major groove on the front tires of a commercial motor vehicle?
choice_a: 4/32 inch
choice_b: 2/32 inch
choice_c: 8/32 inch
choice_d: 1/32 inch
explanation: The manual requires at least 4/32-inch tread depth in every major groove on front tires, and 2/32 inch on other tires, with no fabric showing through.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Tire Problems

question: What is the minimum tread depth required on tires other than the front tires of a CMV?
choice_a: 2/32 inch
choice_b: 4/32 inch
choice_c: 6/32 inch
choice_d: No minimum applies to non-front tires
explanation: Tires other than the front tires must have at least 2/32-inch tread depth, compared to 4/32 inch required on the front tires.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Tire Problems

question: What steering wheel play (measured at the rim of a 20-inch steering wheel) can make a vehicle hard to steer?
choice_a: More than 10 degrees, about 2 inches of movement
choice_b: More than 45 degrees
choice_c: Any play at all, even 1 degree
choice_d: More than 90 degrees
explanation: The manual states that steering wheel play of more than 10 degrees, approximately 2 inches of movement at the rim of a 20-inch wheel, can make a vehicle hard to steer.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Steering System Defects

question: If one-fourth or more of the leaves are missing from a leaf spring, what is the effect on the vehicle's status?
choice_a: It will put the vehicle out of service
choice_b: The vehicle can still be driven with no restrictions
choice_c: Only a warning ticket is issued
choice_d: It only matters if it's the front axle
explanation: Missing or broken leaves in a leaf spring will put the vehicle out of service if one-fourth or more are missing, though the manual notes any defect could be dangerous.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Suspension System Defects

question: Why is a broken exhaust system dangerous, according to the manual?
choice_a: It can let poison fumes into the cab or sleeper berth
choice_b: It always causes an engine fire
choice_c: It automatically triggers an out-of-service violation for excess noise
choice_d: It reduces tire tread life
explanation: A broken exhaust system can let poison fumes into the cab or sleeper berth, so drivers should check for loose, broken, missing, or leaking exhaust parts.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Exhaust System Defects

question: Which of the following is listed as required emergency equipment to check during a vehicle inspection?
choice_a: Fire extinguisher(s) and warning devices such as three reflective triangles
choice_b: A spare tire only
choice_c: A first aid kit is mandatory nationwide
choice_d: Tire chains are always required regardless of season
explanation: Emergency equipment to check includes fire extinguisher(s), spare electrical fuses (unless equipped with circuit breakers), and warning devices such as three reflective triangles or at least 6 fuses or 3 liquid burning flares.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Emergency Equipment

question: During Step 3 of the seven-step inspection method, what should the ABS indicator light do when the engine is started?
choice_a: Come on and then turn off; if it stays on, the ABS is not working properly
choice_b: Stay on continuously the entire trip
choice_c: Flash rapidly whenever the brakes are applied
choice_d: Nothing; ABS lights are not checked during inspection
explanation: When starting the engine, the ABS indicator light should come on and then turn off; if it stays on, the ABS is not working properly.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Seven-Step Inspection Method

question: During Step 3 of the inspection, air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within approximately how much time?
choice_a: 3 minutes
choice_b: 30 seconds
choice_c: 10 minutes
choice_d: 1 minute
explanation: Air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within about 3 minutes, continuing to build to the governor cut-out, usually around 120-140 psi.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Seven-Step Inspection Method

question: In Step 1 of the seven-step inspection method, what should a driver do regarding the last vehicle inspection report?
choice_a: Review it; the motor carrier must repair any items affecting safety and certify that repairs were made or unnecessary
choice_b: Discard it immediately since it is no longer relevant
choice_c: Forward it to the DMV before every trip
choice_d: Only review it if damage is visible from the outside
explanation: Step 1 involves reviewing the last vehicle inspection report; the motor carrier must repair items affecting safety and certify on the report that repairs were made or were unnecessary.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Seven-Step Inspection Method

question: To test hydraulic brakes for leaks during the seven-step inspection, a driver should pump the brake pedal three times, then apply firm pressure and hold it for how long?
choice_a: 5 seconds
choice_b: 30 seconds
choice_c: 1 second
choice_d: 1 minute
explanation: After pumping the pedal three times, the driver applies firm pressure and holds it for five seconds; if the pedal moves, there may be a leak or other problem that must be fixed before driving.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Seven-Step Inspection Method

question: How often must drivers of trucks and truck tractors inspect cargo securement during a trip?
choice_a: Within the first 50 miles, then every 150 miles or every three hours, whichever comes first
choice_b: Only at the start and end of the trip
choice_c: Every 500 miles regardless of time
choice_d: Cargo securement checks are optional once loaded
explanation: The manual requires a cargo securement safety inspection within the first 50 miles of a trip, and then every 150 miles or every three hours after, whichever comes first.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Inspection During a Trip

question: What four basic skills does safe operation of a commercial vehicle require, according to the manual?
choice_a: Accelerating, steering, stopping, and backing safely
choice_b: Parking, fueling, loading, and unloading
choice_c: Signaling, honking, flashing lights, and idling
choice_d: Weighing, inspecting, certifying, and reporting
explanation: The manual identifies accelerating, steering, stopping, and backing safely as the core skills required for safe operation of a commercial vehicle.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Basic Control of Your Vehicle

question: If the drive wheels begin to spin due to poor traction while accelerating, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Take their foot off the accelerator
choice_b: Press the accelerator harder to power through it
choice_c: Apply the parking brake immediately
choice_d: Shift into a higher gear immediately
explanation: If the drive wheels begin to spin from too much power on poor traction, the driver should take their foot off the accelerator to regain control.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Accelerating

question: How should a driver hold the steering wheel to maintain a firm hold in case of hitting a curb or pothole?
choice_a: With both hands on opposite sides of the wheel
choice_b: With one hand at the top of the wheel
choice_c: With both hands close together at the bottom
choice_d: Hand position does not matter for control
explanation: The manual advises holding the steering wheel firmly with both hands on opposite sides so the wheel cannot be pulled away from your hands if you hit a curb or pothole.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Steering

question: What are the five basic safety rules for backing a commercial vehicle listed in the manual?
choice_a: Start in the proper position, look at your path, use mirrors on both sides, back slowly, and back toward the driver's side
choice_b: Honk continuously, use hazard lights, back quickly, use one mirror, and back toward the passenger side
choice_c: Only use a spotter, no other precautions are needed
choice_d: Back only at night for better visibility
explanation: The manual lists five key safety rules for backing: start in the proper position, look at your path, use mirrors on both sides, back slowly, and back and turn toward the driver's side whenever possible.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Backing Safely

question: Why does the manual recommend backing and turning toward the driver's side whenever possible, even if it means going around the block?
choice_a: The driver can watch the rear of the vehicle by looking out the side window, providing better visibility
choice_b: It is required by federal law in all 50 states
choice_c: It reduces fuel consumption
choice_d: It is faster than backing toward the passenger side
explanation: Backing toward the driver's side lets the driver watch the rear of the vehicle through the side window; backing toward the right side is dangerous because visibility is much worse.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Backing Safely

question: When using a helper to back a commercial vehicle, what should the driver and helper agree upon before starting?
choice_a: A set of hand signals, including a signal for 'stop'
choice_b: A verbal countdown only, no hand signals
choice_c: Nothing in advance; the helper should improvise
choice_d: A radio frequency to communicate on
explanation: Before backing, the driver and helper should work out a set of hand signals they both understand, including agreeing on a signal for 'stop.'
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Backing Safely

question: Most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized manual transmissions require what technique to change gears?
choice_a: Double clutching
choice_b: Single clutching only
choice_c: No clutch use at all
choice_d: Clutch braking exclusively
explanation: Most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized manual transmissions require double clutching to change gears; synchronized manual transmissions do not require it.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Manual Transmissions

question: According to the manual, what are the two ways of knowing when to shift up a manual transmission?
choice_a: Using engine speed (rpm) via the tachometer, or road speed (mph) via the speedometer
choice_b: Using the odometer or the fuel gauge
choice_c: Counting seconds since the last shift only
choice_d: Listening for the horn only
explanation: Drivers can shift up based on engine speed (rpm), watched on the tachometer, or road speed (mph), watched on the speedometer; some drivers also learn to use engine sounds.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Shifting Gears

question: Before starting down a hill, why should a driver downshift to a lower gear before beginning the descent?
choice_a: To control speed without using the brakes hard, since overheating brakes can lose their braking power
choice_b: To save fuel only
choice_c: It has no safety benefit, only a comfort benefit
choice_d: To reduce engine noise
explanation: Downshifting before a hill lets the driver control speed without hard braking, since heavy braking can overheat the brakes and cause them to lose their braking power.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Shifting Gears, Downshifting

question: Why should a driver downshift to the right gear before entering a curve, rather than during it?
choice_a: It lets the driver use some power through the curve for stability and to speed up as soon as they are out of the curve
choice_b: It is only a cosmetic habit with no safety benefit
choice_c: It prevents the transmission from overheating
choice_d: It is required only for automatic transmissions
explanation: Downshifting before entering a curve lets the driver use some power through the curve to help the vehicle remain stable, and allows speeding up once out of the curve.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Shifting Gears, Downshifting

question: How many basic types of retarders does the manual describe?
choice_a: Four -- exhaust, engine, hydraulic, and electric
choice_b: Two -- mechanical and hydraulic only
choice_c: Six types, including a magnetic type
choice_d: Only one universal type
explanation: The manual describes four basic types of retarders: exhaust, engine, hydraulic, and electric, all of which can be turned on or off by the driver.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Retarders

question: When should a driver turn off a retarder, according to the manual's caution?
choice_a: Whenever the road is wet, icy, or snow covered
choice_b: Only when parked
choice_c: Retarders should never be turned off once activated
choice_d: Only during daytime driving
explanation: Because a retarder can cause drive wheels with poor traction to skid, the manual advises turning the retarder off whenever the road is wet, icy, or snow covered.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Retarders

question: How far ahead does the manual say most good drivers should look while driving?
choice_a: 12 to 15 seconds ahead
choice_b: 2 to 3 seconds ahead
choice_c: 30 to 45 seconds ahead
choice_d: 5 to 6 seconds ahead
explanation: Most good drivers look at least 12 to 15 seconds ahead, which is about one block at low speeds and about a quarter mile at highway speeds.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Seeing Ahead

question: At highway speeds, looking 12 to 15 seconds ahead corresponds to approximately what distance?
choice_a: About a quarter of a mile
choice_b: About one city block
choice_c: About 50 feet
choice_d: About 5 miles
explanation: At highway speeds, looking 12 to 15 seconds ahead means looking about a quarter of a mile down the road; at lower speeds, it is about one block.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Seeing Ahead

question: When should mirror adjustment be checked, according to the manual?
choice_a: Prior to the start of any trip, and it can only be checked accurately when the trailer(s) are straight
choice_b: Only once per year at inspection time
choice_c: Only after an accident
choice_d: Mirror adjustment never needs checking once set
explanation: Mirror adjustment should be checked before the start of any trip and can only be checked accurately when the trailer(s) are straight.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Seeing to the Sides and Rear

question: When changing lanes, at what points should a driver check the mirrors?
choice_a: Before signaling, after signaling to check the blind spot, right after starting the change, and after completing it
choice_b: Only once, immediately before signaling
choice_c: Only after the lane change is complete
choice_d: Mirror checks are not necessary if using turn signals
explanation: The manual recommends checking mirrors before changing lanes for room, after signaling to check the blind spot, right after starting the change to double-check, and after completing the change.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Seeing to the Sides and Rear

question: What is a key characteristic of convex ('fisheye,' 'spot,' or 'bug-eye') mirrors that drivers must account for?
choice_a: Everything appears smaller and farther away than it really is
choice_b: They only show what is directly behind the vehicle
choice_c: They eliminate all blind spots completely
choice_d: They cannot be used on trailers
explanation: Convex mirrors show a wider area than flat mirrors, but everything appears smaller and farther away than it really is, so drivers must allow for this distortion.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Seeing to the Sides and Rear

question: Why should a driver check mirrors quickly rather than focusing on them for a long time while driving?
choice_a: Focusing too long on the mirrors means traveling a distance without knowing what is happening ahead
choice_b: Long mirror checks damage the mirror's adjustment mechanism
choice_c: It is only a legal requirement, not a safety concern
choice_d: Extended mirror checks are illegal in Kentucky
explanation: The manual warns that focusing on the mirrors too long means the vehicle will travel a distance without the driver knowing what is happening ahead.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Seeing to the Sides and Rear

question: What are the three good rules for using turn signals listed in the manual?
choice_a: Signal early, signal continuously, and cancel your signal
choice_b: Signal loudly, signal briefly, and signal twice
choice_c: Signal only at intersections, never on the highway
choice_d: Signal only when other vehicles are visible
explanation: The three rules are: signal early to keep others from trying to pass you, signal continuously and don't cancel until the turn is complete, and cancel your signal after turning if it doesn't self-cancel.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Communicating, Turns

question: How can a driver warn following drivers that they will need to slow down?
choice_a: A few light taps on the brake pedal to flash the brake lights
choice_b: Turning off all lights briefly
choice_c: Sounding the horn continuously
choice_d: Rolling down the window and waving
explanation: A few light taps on the brake pedal, enough to flash the brake lights, warns following drivers that you will need to slow down.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Communicating, Slowing Down

question: When passing a vehicle, pedestrian, or bicyclist, what should a driver assume, according to the manual?
choice_a: That they don't see you, and drive carefully enough to avoid a crash even if they don't see or hear you
choice_b: That they always see and hear you clearly
choice_c: That honking is unnecessary in every situation
choice_d: That they will always yield the right of way
explanation: Whenever about to pass a vehicle, pedestrian, or bicyclist, assume they don't see you; tap the horn lightly or flash lights when legal, and drive to avoid a crash regardless.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Communicating Your Presence

question: If a driver must stop on or by a road or shoulder, within how many minutes must warning devices be put out?
choice_a: 10 minutes
choice_b: 30 minutes
choice_c: 2 minutes
choice_d: 60 minutes
explanation: If a driver must stop on a road or shoulder, emergency warning devices must be put out within ten minutes.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Communicating Your Presence

question: When stopped on a one-way or divided highway, where should warning devices be placed?
choice_a: 10 feet, 100 feet, and 200 feet toward the approaching traffic
choice_b: Only 50 feet behind the vehicle
choice_c: Directly under the vehicle only
choice_d: 1,000 feet in front of the vehicle only
explanation: On a one-way or divided highway, warning devices should be placed 10 feet, 100 feet, and 200 feet toward the approaching traffic.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Communicating Your Presence

question: If a hill, curve, or other obstruction prevents drivers from seeing a stopped vehicle within 500 feet, what should be done with the rearmost warning triangle?
choice_a: Move it back down the road so warning is provided before the obstruction
choice_b: Remove it entirely since it cannot be seen anyway
choice_c: Place it directly on top of the vehicle
choice_d: It does not need to be moved
explanation: If line of sight is obstructed by a hill or curve, the rear-most triangle should be moved back beyond the obstruction so warning is provided to approaching traffic.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Communicating Your Presence

question: What are the three components that add up to total stopping distance?
choice_a: Perception distance, reaction distance, and braking distance
choice_b: Acceleration distance, cruising distance, and coasting distance
choice_c: Signal distance, mirror-check distance, and horn distance
choice_d: Visibility distance, weather distance, and traction distance
explanation: Total stopping distance is the sum of perception distance, reaction distance, and braking distance.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Stopping Distance

question: At 55 mph, what is the total minimum stopping distance, combining perception, reaction, and braking distance?
choice_a: 419 feet
choice_b: 216 feet
choice_c: 300 feet
choice_d: 142 feet
explanation: At 55 mph, the vehicle's total minimum stopping distance, including perception, reaction, and braking distance, is 419 feet.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Stopping Distance

question: When speed is doubled from 20 to 40 mph, how much greater is the impact and braking distance?
choice_a: 4 times greater
choice_b: 2 times greater
choice_c: 9 times greater
choice_d: 16 times greater
explanation: Doubling speed from 20 to 40 mph makes the impact 4 times greater, and the braking distance is also 4 times longer.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Stopping Distance

question: Why do empty trucks require greater stopping distances than fully loaded trucks?
choice_a: An empty vehicle has less traction; brakes, tires, springs, and shocks are designed to work best when fully loaded
choice_b: Empty trucks always have worn-out brakes
choice_c: Empty trucks travel faster on average
choice_d: There is no difference in stopping distance based on load
explanation: Empty trucks require greater stopping distances because an empty vehicle has less traction; heavy-vehicle brakes, tires, springs, and shocks are designed to work best when the vehicle is fully loaded.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Stopping Distance

question: On a wet road, the manual recommends reducing speed by about how much compared to dry-road speed?
choice_a: About one-third (for example, from 55 to about 35 mph)
choice_b: About one-tenth
choice_c: No reduction is necessary on wet roads
choice_d: About two-thirds
explanation: The manual recommends reducing speed by about one-third on a wet road, such as slowing from 55 to about 35 mph, since wet roads can double stopping distance.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Matching Speed to the Road Surface

question: What is 'black ice,' as described in the manual?
choice_a: A thin, clear layer of ice that makes the road look wet, common when temperatures are below freezing
choice_b: Ice that has been mixed with road tar
choice_c: A type of tire compound used in winter tires
choice_d: Ice found only on bridges, never on regular roads
explanation: Black ice is a thin, clear layer of ice that makes the road look wet; any time the temperature is below freezing and the road looks wet, drivers should watch for black ice.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Matching Speed to the Road Surface

question: If a vehicle begins to hydroplane, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Release the accelerator and push in the clutch, letting the wheels turn freely, without using the brakes
choice_b: Immediately apply the brakes hard to regain traction
choice_c: Turn the steering wheel sharply to break the water film
choice_d: Accelerate to punch through the water
explanation: If hydroplaning, the driver should release the accelerator and push in the clutch to slow the vehicle and let the wheels turn freely; the manual specifically warns not to use the brakes to slow down while hydroplaning.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Matching Speed to the Road Surface

question: According to the manual, trucks with a high center of gravity can roll over even when:
choice_a: Driven at the posted speed limit for a curve
choice_b: Parked on level ground
choice_c: Driven well below the posted speed limit on a straight road
choice_d: Empty and unloaded
explanation: Tests have shown that trucks with a high center of gravity can roll over at the posted speed limit for a curve, so drivers must slow further than the posted limit in many cases.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Speed and Curves

question: What is the general rule for how much following distance to leave ahead at speeds below 40 mph?
choice_a: At least one second for each 10 feet of vehicle length
choice_b: A fixed 2 seconds regardless of vehicle length
choice_c: One second for every 50 feet of vehicle length
choice_d: No specific rule is given for space ahead
explanation: The manual's rule of thumb is at least one second of following distance for each 10 feet of vehicle length at speeds below 40 mph.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Space Ahead

question: At speeds greater than 40 mph, how should the following distance rule be adjusted?
choice_a: Add 1 additional second for safety
choice_b: Cut the following distance in half
choice_c: No adjustment is needed above 40 mph
choice_d: Add 5 additional seconds
explanation: At speeds greater than 40 mph, the manual instructs drivers to add 1 additional second to the following-distance calculation for safety.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Space Ahead

question: What is one recommended way to reduce the chances of a crash when being tailgated?
choice_a: Increase your own following distance to give more room to react
choice_b: Speed up to get away from the tailgater
choice_c: Tap the brakes repeatedly to warn them off
choice_d: Flash your taillights on and off rapidly
explanation: The manual recommends increasing your following distance when tailgated, which helps avoid sudden speed or direction changes and makes it easier for the tailgater to pass; it explicitly warns against tricks like flashing lights.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Space Behind

question: When making a right turn in a vehicle too large to complete it without swinging into another lane, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Turn wide as the turn is completed, keeping the rear of the vehicle close to the curb
choice_b: Swing wide to the left before starting the turn
choice_c: Stop completely in the intersection and wait for a gap
choice_d: Always use the far-left lane to start the turn
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to turn wide as they complete the turn, keeping the rear close to the curb, which stops other drivers from passing on the right; swinging wide to the left at the start risks a following driver trying to pass on the right.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Space for Turns

question: On a left turn, what should a driver do before starting to turn, to avoid off-tracking into another vehicle?
choice_a: Make sure they have reached the center of the intersection before starting the left turn
choice_b: Start the turn from the far right lane
choice_c: Turn as early as possible before entering the intersection
choice_d: Off-tracking is not a concern on left turns
explanation: On a left turn, the driver should reach the center of the intersection before starting the turn; turning too soon can cause the vehicle's left side to hit another vehicle due to off-tracking.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Space for Turns

question: If there are two turning lanes available for a turn, which lane should a commercial driver use?
choice_a: The right turn lane, since drivers on your left can be more readily seen
choice_b: The inside (left) turn lane, to complete the turn faster
choice_c: Either lane, it makes no difference
choice_d: Whichever lane has less traffic, regardless of position
explanation: With two turning lanes, drivers should always take the right turn lane; starting in the inside lane may require swinging right to complete the turn, and drivers on the left are more easily seen from the right lane.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Space for Turns

question: How does the manual define a 'hazard'?
choice_a: Any road condition or other road user that is a possible danger
choice_b: Only an object that has already caused a crash
choice_c: Only weather-related conditions
choice_d: A hazard is only relevant to passenger vehicles, not CMVs
explanation: A hazard is defined as any road condition or other road user, such as a driver, bicyclist, or pedestrian, that is a possible danger.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Importance of Seeing Hazards

question: Why does seeing a hazard early, before it becomes an emergency, reduce danger?
choice_a: It gives the driver more time to act, whereas sudden braking or lane changes are more likely to lead to a crash
choice_b: It has no effect on crash risk, only on fuel economy
choice_c: It only matters for the vehicle behind you
choice_d: Early hazard recognition only matters in fog
explanation: Seeing hazards before they become emergencies gives the driver more time to prepare; a driver forced into sudden braking or a quick lane change is much more likely to cause a crash.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Importance of Seeing Hazards

question: Which of the following is listed as a hazard clue related to a driver's vision being blocked?
choice_a: Vans, loaded station wagons, and vehicles with frosted or snow-covered windows
choice_b: Any vehicle painted a bright color
choice_c: Vehicles with tinted headlights
choice_d: Only motorcycles, since they are small
explanation: The manual lists vans, loaded station wagons, cars with blocked rear windows, rental trucks, and vehicles with frosted, ice-covered, or snow-covered windows as hazard clues involving blocked vision.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: What is the 'slow moving vehicle' symbol described in the manual, used to warn of vehicles like farm machinery and construction equipment?
choice_a: A red triangle with an orange center
choice_b: A yellow diamond with a black border
choice_c: A blue circle with a white arrow
choice_d: A green square with white text
explanation: The slow-moving-vehicle symbol is a red triangle with an orange center, used to warn other drivers of naturally slow vehicles such as mopeds, farm machinery, and tractors.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: What clues suggest a driver may be impaired (sleepy, drunk, on drugs, or ill), according to the manual?
choice_a: Weaving across the road, drifting, stopping at the wrong time, or an open window in cold weather
choice_b: Driving exactly at the speed limit at all times
choice_c: Using turn signals for every lane change
choice_d: Keeping a large following distance
explanation: Impaired driver clues include weaving or drifting across the road, leaving the road, stopping at the wrong time (such as at a green light), and having a window open in cold weather.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: When are you considered to be 'in conflict' with another road user, according to the manual?
choice_a: When you have to change speed and/or direction to avoid hitting someone
choice_b: Only when a citation has been issued
choice_c: Only after a collision has occurred
choice_d: Conflicts only occur on multi-lane highways
explanation: A conflict occurs when a driver has to change speed and/or direction to avoid hitting someone, such as at intersections, merges, or forced lane changes.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: What should a driver do after recognizing a potential hazard, according to the guidance on 'Always Have a Plan'?
choice_a: Think about what emergencies could develop and figure out what action to take
choice_b: Ignore it unless it becomes an immediate emergency
choice_c: Only react after the hazard causes another driver to react first
choice_d: Report it to dispatch before taking any action
explanation: When a driver sees a hazard, the manual advises thinking about the emergencies that could develop and figuring out a planned response, making the driver a prepared, defensive driver.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Always Have a Plan

question: According to the Large Truck Crash Causation Study (LTCCS) cited in the manual, what percentage of large-truck crashes occurred when the CMV driver was externally distracted?
choice_a: 8 percent
choice_b: 2 percent
choice_c: 23 percent
choice_d: 39 percent
explanation: The LTCCS reported that 8 percent of large-truck crashes occurred when the CMV driver was externally distracted, and 2 percent occurred when internally distracted.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, The Distracted Driving Crash Problem

question: According to NHTSA data cited in the manual, approximately how many people are killed each year on U.S. roadways in crashes involving distracted driving?
choice_a: About 5,500
choice_b: About 500
choice_c: About 50,000
choice_d: About 448,000
explanation: The manual cites NHTSA data that approximately 5,500 people are killed each year, and an estimated 448,000 are injured, in crashes involving distracted driving.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, The Distracted Driving Crash Problem

question: According to research cited in the manual, talking on a cell phone, even hands-free, saps the brain of what percentage of the energy it would normally devote to safe driving?
choice_a: 39 percent
choice_b: 8 percent
choice_c: 60 percent
choice_d: 10 percent
explanation: Research cited in the manual indicates that talking on a cell phone, even hands-free, saps the brain of 39 percent of the energy it would ordinarily devote to safe driving.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, The Distracted Driving Crash Problem

question: Why does the manual describe activities like talking on a cell phone or texting as posing an even greater crash risk than a purely physical or purely mental distraction alone?
choice_a: They combine both physical and mental distraction at the same time
choice_b: They are technically illegal in all 50 states without exception
choice_c: They only distract passengers, not drivers
choice_d: There is no additional risk compared to a single-type distraction
explanation: Activities such as talking on a cell phone or texting combine both physical and mental distraction simultaneously, creating an even greater chance that a crash could happen.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Types of Distractions

question: Under the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations, how many convictions of hand-held mobile telephone use while operating a CMV result in disqualification?
choice_a: Two or more convictions
choice_b: Only one conviction
choice_c: Five or more convictions
choice_d: Hand-held phone use never results in disqualification
explanation: A CDL is disqualified after two or more convictions of any state law on hand-held mobile telephone use while operating a CMV: 60 days for the second offense within 3 years, and 120 days for three or more offenses within 3 years.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Cell/Mobile Phones

question: According to research cited in the manual, dialing drivers took their eyes off the forward roadway for an average of how long, and how far does that equate to at 55 mph?
choice_a: 3.8 seconds, about 306 feet -- roughly the length of a football field
choice_b: 1 second, about 80 feet
choice_c: 10 seconds, about 800 feet
choice_d: 0.5 seconds, about 40 feet
explanation: Research found dialing drivers took their eyes off the road for an average of 3.8 seconds, which at 55 mph (80.7 feet per second) equates to about 306 feet, roughly a football field, without looking at the roadway.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Cell/Mobile Phones

question: How does the manual define 'texting' for purposes of the CMV texting prohibition?
choice_a: Manually entering text into, or reading text from, an electronic device, including SMS, email, instant messaging, or web page access requests
choice_b: Only sending traditional SMS text messages, not email
choice_c: Only reading text, never entering it
choice_d: Any use of a smartphone, including phone calls
explanation: Texting is defined as manually entering text into, or reading text from, an electronic device, including SMS, email, instant messaging, requesting a web page, or other electronic text retrieval or entry.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Texting

question: Research cited in the manual found that texting increases the odds of a safety-critical event (crash, near-crash, or unintentional lane deviation) by approximately how much?
choice_a: 23.2 times greater
choice_b: 6 times greater
choice_c: 2 times greater
choice_d: 39 times greater
explanation: Research shows the odds of a safety-critical event are 23.2 times greater for drivers who are texting compared to those who are not.
source_note: Kentucky Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: September 9, 2022, Kentucky-specific content revised 12/2024), Kentucky State Police / Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) Division of Driver Licensing -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Texting
